{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-sonnet-5","id":"msg_011Cg2NnTCe8fiCkSmRLZXDb","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The lighthouse keeper's log at Caldrick Point hadn't been written in by human hand for eleven years, not since the automation crews came through with their diesel generators and their solid-state relays and took away the last man who knew how to trim a wick. But Edda Vossler still climbed the hundred and forty-three steps every morning, because someone had to check that the machine remembered what it was for.

She was not, technically, a lighthouse keeper. The agency called her a "maintenance liaison," which meant she drove out from the mainland twice a week in a boat that smelled like diesel and old rope, and she climbed the stairs, and she looked at gauges, and she wrote numbers in a tablet that uploaded itself to a server in a city she had never seen. The light did its own work now. It knew when to turn on. It knew how bright to burn depending on the fog density, which it measured with a sensor no bigger than a shirt button. It had not needed Edda, or anyone, in eleven years.

And yet.

On the morning this story begins, Edda climbed the stairs and found the light already on, though it was ten in the morning and the fog had not yet rolled in. She stood in the lamp room with her hand on the cold iron rail and watched the beam turn, slow and patient, sweeping the empty grey water where no ships needed guiding at this hour, past the gulls that didn't flinch because they'd long since stopped fearing the light as an omen, and back around to find her again.

She checked the log. No malfunction recorded. No fog warning triggered. The light had simply decided, on its own schedule, to burn.

"You're early," she said to it, because eleven years of solitary maintenance runs will make a person talk to machinery, and because some nights, out here, talking to the machinery felt less foolish than talking to herself.

The light did not answer, of course. Lighthouses have never answered anyone, not really, not even in the old days when a keeper lived in the squat stone house at the base and trimmed the wick every four hours through the night and filled the oil reservoir with hands that smelled permanently of kerosene. The keepers talked to the light the way sailors talk to the sea, the way farmers talk to weather — not expecting response, only expecting to be heard by something larger than themselves, something that had outlasted every person who'd ever stood beside it and would outlast everyone yet to come.

Edda had read the old logs, the paper ones, preserved now in a climate-controlled room at the historical society because someone decided a hundred years of a keeper's handwriting was worth preserving, unlike the keeper himself. Thomas Reyes, 1911 to 1938, twenty-seven years at Caldrick Point, had written things like: *Fog thick as wool all night. Kept her burning. Boy from the mainland came for supplies, says there's been a war started somewhere. Can't imagine it reaches here.* And later: *Wick trimmed. Reservoir full. My wife says the baby kicked today. I told her I'd be home by solstice.*

The light had burned through two wars and the deaths of four keepers and the births of nineteen children born to keepers' wives in the little house, and through all of it the beam had turned, patient, indifferent, doing the one thing it existed to do: say *here is land, here is rock, here is the edge of the world, steer clear or steer toward, your choice, but at least now you know where you are.*

Edda sat down on the iron stairs, because something about the light being on without reason unsettled her in a way she didn't examine too closely, and she thought about her grandmother, who had grown up two coves over and told Edda once, when Edda was young enough to be frightened of the dark, that lighthouses were built because the sea doesn't care if you live or die, but people do, and a lighthouse is just a very large, very patient way of a person saying *I care, even from this distance, even if I never meet you, even if you never know my name.*

Her grandmother had not been a religious woman, but she had treated lighthouses the way some people treat churches: with a quiet, specific reverence, a sense that the structure meant more than its function. A radio buoy could warn a ship off rocks. A lighthouse did something else besides. It stood. It was seen. From a dark deck in a worse storm than you'd ever admit to your crew, you could look toward shore and see, not safety exactly, but evidence — evidence that humans had been here before you, had anticipated your fear, had built something tall and stubborn specifically to meet you in your worst moment with a steady, wordless *I see you.*

Edda's radio crackled. It was Marsh, from the agency, asking why the beacon at Caldrick had triggered an unscheduled activation alert.

"I don't know," she said. "It's just on. No fog. No ships logged in the channel."

"Probably a sensor fault. Log it and reset the cycle."

"I will." She did not reset it yet. She sat a while longer, watching the beam pass over the water, because resetting it felt, in that moment, like interrupting someone mid-sentence.

She thought about the ships that didn't need it anymore — satellite positioning accurate to the meter, radar that saw through fog better than any human eye, charts updated in real time, hulls equipped with collision-avoidance systems that made the old business of squinting into darkness for a flashing light almost quaint, the way a sundial is quaint next to a wristwatch. Caldrick Point's light had not actually prevented a wreck in thirty-one years. The agency kept it running mostly because decommissioning a historic lighthouse required paperwork nobody wanted to process, and because the handful of fishing boats still working these waters liked having it there, the way people like having their childhood home still standing even after they've moved away and have no plans to return.

But maybe that was the thing her grandmother meant. Maybe a lighthouse's real work was never really about the ships at all — not anymore, maybe not ever fully. Maybe it was about this: a tall white tower on a rock at the edge of the water, burning because burning is what it was built to do, regardless of whether anyone needed the light to find their way home. Maybe it burned for the two sailors three hundred years ago whose boat went down in a squall not two miles from here, their names lost, their bodies never found, no light built in time to save them, only built after, as if the structure itself were an apology carved in granite and glass. Maybe it burned because building something permanent in a place defined by impermanence — rock worn down by tide, coastline redrawn by every storm, the sea itself a thing that erases rather than preserves — was its own kind of defiance.

Edda stood up. She walked to the great lamp and put her palm flat against the warm glass, feeling the vibration of the mechanism turning beneath her hand, patient as a held breath.

"Burn, then," she said. "Nobody's stopping you."

She logged the activation as a sensor anomaly, because that was true enough for the agency's purposes, and she did not reset the cycle. She climbed back down the hundred and forty-three steps, got in her boat, and motored back toward the mainland, and when she looked back from a half mile out, the light was still turning, sweeping its slow circle over water that didn't need it, over gulls that ignored it, over a coastline that had long since learned to find its own way.

But it turned anyway. It would turn tonight, and tomorrow, and the night after, long after Edda's contract with the agency ended, long after the agency itself was dissolved and replaced by some newer bureaucracy with some newer name, because that is the nature of a lighthouse: it does not ask whether it is needed.
